about: The same five synthetic test viewers, shown v0.5 (stills and narration, through OpenRouter). Not people and not a review signature. The audience Dinis Cruz named is people who know Agile. Em dashes in their answers are replaced by commas.

viewers.who: a Scrum Master in a 300-person company that adopted a scaled Agile framework two years ago; you feel the ceremonies have grown and the values have faded. Sceptical of buzzwords.

answer.why_stop: The Martin Fowler quote about the 'Agile Industrial Complex' hits me right where it hurts while I'm drowning in two-week sprint cadences and quarterly PI planning theater.
answer.why_drop: You had me until you claimed an 'Agile' unit has 'twenty, thirty, fifty roles' and an 'org chart for one task.' That's not agile values; that's automated bureaucratic bloat masquerading as progress.
answer.story_back: The video claims to rescue Agile from corporate bureaucracy by replacing teams with ephemeral swarms of AI agents and nested org charts organized around single tasks.
confusing: Quoting 'individuals and interactions over processes and tools' right before pitching an entirely tool-driven system of AI bots and text files.
Calling an org chart of 50 roles for a single task 'agile' with a straight face.
The diagram in Scene 6 and 7 looking like an unreadable cloud infrastructure map rather than any recognizable team structure.
answer.best_moment: Scene 1 calling out the Agile Industrial Complex imposing methods upon people, 100% truth.
answer.one_change: Stop co-opting the Agile Manifesto to hawk AI agent prompt chains; if you're building automated workflow scripts for LLMs, just call it workflow automation.
answer.weakest_moment: Scene 5 showing an org chart expanding to 50 nodes for 'one task', it triggered my fight-or-flight response.
answer.what_i_would_do_tomorrow: Roll my eyes, close the app, and prepare for our retro where nobody talks about how much time we waste on Jira tickets.

viewers.who: a founder of a 6-person startup who uses AI coding agents daily and wonders how to organise more of them. Impatient; scrolls fast on LinkedIn.

answer.why_stop: The AI-agent org-chart visuals and the promise of scaling a tiny team are immediately relevant to me.
answer.why_drop: It shifts from a concrete idea into glowing org charts, arbitrary role counts, and jargon. I still do not know how I would actually run a cell.
answer.story_back: Agile Cells are temporary, file-defined teams of people and AI agents assembled for one task, then shut down and archived.
confusing: What exactly is an agent allowed to do?
Who makes decisions when agents disagree?
Why are there 10, 20, or 50 roles for one task?
What does 'taken down' mean operationally?
How is this different from an ordinary multi-agent workflow?
answer.best_moment: The real session-refresh example with the before-and-after process and concrete roles.
answer.one_change: Replace the abstract role-count and org-chart sequence with one concrete end-to-end cell run showing the files, agent handoffs, human decisions, and final output.
answer.weakest_moment: The repeated manifesto slide; it spends too long restating the same four values without connecting them to the proposed system.
answer.what_i_would_do_tomorrow: Click through to the actual cell files or workflow, but I would not share the film as-is.

viewers.who: a CTO at a mid-sized firm who buys outsourced work (websites, CRM set-up, social media). You want to know what you could actually buy and whether it is real.

answer.why_stop: The Martin Fowler quote shitting on the 'Agile Industrial Complex' catches my eye because I spend millions on certified Scrum clowns who deliver nothing.
answer.why_drop: You promised to show me how this works 'for real' to deliver actual work, and by Scene 6 your grand proof of concept is... making a short marketing video about Claude sessions. You automated making TikToks with LLMs, not shipping production software.
answer.story_back: The video claims you can scale original Agile principles by spinning up temporary org charts of human workers and AI agents that tackle a single task and disband once the files are committed.
confusing: What am I actually buying: a SaaS orchestrator, an outsourced dev agency, or an open-source GitHub framework?
Scene 7 has names like 'Dinis Cruz', 'c.maestro', and 'higgsfield.b' thrown on an org chart without explaining who owns the code, QA, or security liabilities.
Why you wasted 9 seconds reciting the 2001 Agile Manifesto to a tech buyer who already knows it by heart.
answer.best_moment: Scene 7 showing the actual agent hierarchy (orchestrator, critic, test viewers using GPT/Gemini) because it finally hints at a real technical workflow.
answer.one_change: Cut the Agile history lesson and show an agent cell actually refactoring a legacy codebase or standing up a CRM workflow instead of generating an AI video.
answer.weakest_moment: Scene 3 displaying the yellow sticky-note Agile values over a cartoon building like a mandatory HR onboarding slide.
answer.what_i_would_do_tomorrow: Keep scrolling and forget about it; this looks like academic AI agent architecture porn with zero commercial viability for real enterprise outsourcing.

viewers.who: a developer who has done Agile since 2005, read the Manifesto many times, and dislikes people misquoting it.

answer.why_stop: The Martin Fowler quote is a credible, sharp hook, and the visual language looks more intentional than the usual Agile explainer.
answer.story_back: Agile Cells proposes temporary, transparent teams of people and agents that form around one task, deliver it, and then dissolve.
confusing: The film never clearly defines what an agent is or how agents differ from people.
It jumps from the Manifesto's values to a specific cell architecture without explaining why that architecture follows from those values.
The claims that one cell made a real film and that Agile can scale are asserted rather than demonstrated.
The 10, 20, 30, and 50-role examples feel like organizational diagrams, not evidence of a working method.
The phrase "Agile Cells" sounds like a branded process imposed on people, which clashes with Fowler's opening criticism unless the distinction is made explicit.
answer.best_moment: Scene 6, where the abstract cell becomes concrete through the refresh-a-session film and its visible before-and-after result.
answer.one_change: Start with the real one-day film outcome, then explain how the temporary cell produced it and explicitly connect that design to the Manifesto's four values.
answer.weakest_moment: The opening spends 11 seconds repeating essentially the same Fowler quote frame, which is visually static and delays the actual idea.
answer.what_i_would_do_tomorrow: Read the linked cell files and look for a concrete example showing what the agents actually did and how the result was evaluated.

viewers.who: someone who does not work in software, scrolling Instagram Reels in the evening, watching with sound off.

answer.why_stop: The giant glowing auditorium in the first frame looked like a dark sci-fi movie for half a second.
answer.why_drop: I read the phrase 'Agile Industrial Complex' and realized this is some boring LinkedIn corporate tech lecture that accidentally ended up on my feed.
answer.story_back: It is trying to sell some corporate productivity framework where you set up temporary teams of AI bots to finish a project.
confusing: What on earth is an 'Agile Cell'?
Who is Martin Fowler and why should anyone care what he said in 2018?
What are 'agents' here, software, bots, or actual people?
The random slide about 'managing your Claude sessions' with huge 8-digit numbers makes zero sense.
answer.best_moment: The initial perspective shot of the dark arena with glowing desks before the text ruins it.
answer.one_change: Delete the entire video from Instagram and post it where software project managers actually hang out, because regular people do not want to see org charts after work.
answer.weakest_moment: Scene 3, which is literally just a giant beige sticky note filled with corporate buzzwords.
answer.what_i_would_do_tomorrow: Swipe up immediately to find a meme or a recipe video.

what_they_agree_on: The agile veteran watches to the end; the scrum master, the founder and the buyer now stay to 38 to 42 seconds (v0.4: 26 to 35).
The new opening works for the Agile audience: the scrum master names Fowler's line as the best moment.
Still named as weakest: the 50-role chart (Dinis's own message) and the Manifesto page (kept at his word). The veteran finds the Fowler frame static for its 10 seconds.
